clinicalPearls: Polyhydramnios is an excessive volume of amniotic fluid, defined sonographically by a deepest vertical pool at or above a defined threshold or an amniotic fluid index above the ninety-fifth centile for gestation
Causes fall into fetal, maternal, and placental groups; roughly half to two-thirds are idiopathic, but a cause should always be sought

Fetal causes include anything that impairs swallowing or increases urine output, such as gastrointestinal obstruction (oesophageal or duodenal atresia), neurological and neuromuscular disorders, orofacial clefts, chest masses, cardiac anomalies, and hydrops
Maternal diabetes, pre-existing or gestational, is a leading maternal cause through fetal hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis, so glycaemic control should be assessed
In monochorionic twins, polyhydramnios in one sac with oligohydramnios in the other suggests twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Symptoms and signs reflect uterine overdistension: abdominal discomfort and breathlessness, a large-for-dates uterus, a tense abdomen with difficulty palpating fetal parts, and a fluid thrill

Complications arise chiefly from overdistension and sudden decompression, including preterm labour, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, malpresentation, cord prolapse, placental abruption after membrane rupture, and postpartum haemorrhage from atony

Management targets the cause and the complications: optimise maternal glycaemia, monitor for preterm labour and malpresentation, consider amnioreduction in symptomatic cases, and assess the neonate for anomalies such as oesophageal atresia after birth
reference.pathophysiology: Amniotic fluid volume in the second half of pregnancy is maintained by a balance between fetal urine production and lung fluid, which add fluid, and fetal swallowing and intramembranous absorption, which remove it. Polyhydramnios develops when production exceeds removal. Reduced swallowing or absorption occurs with upper gastrointestinal obstruction, in which the fetus cannot swallow fluid past an atresia, with neuromuscular disease impairing swallowing, and with external compression of the gut. Increased production occurs with fetal polyuria, as in maternal hyperglycaemia causing fetal osmotic diuresis, in high-output states such as fetal anaemia, and in the recipient twin of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. The accumulating fluid overdistends the uterus, stretching the myometrium and predisposing to preterm contractions and, after membrane rupture, to rapid decompression that can shear the placenta or allow the cord to prolapse.
additionalDifferentials: Large uterine fibroids or an adnexal mass
Maternal obesity giving a false impression of a large uterus
An ovarian or other pelvic-abdominal cyst
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound quantification of amniotic fluid by deepest vertical pool or amniotic fluid index
Detailed fetal anomaly ultrasound, with attention to the stomach bubble, swallowing, and structural survey
Maternal testing for diabetes by glucose tolerance testing or glycaemic assessment
Assessment for fetal anaemia, such as middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler, and for hydrops
Screening for congenital infection where indicated
Consideration of fetal karyotype or microarray when structural anomalies are present
Assessment of chorionicity and inter-twin fluid discordance in multiple pregnancy
redFlags: Rapidly increasing fluid or acute maternal respiratory distress from massive polyhydramnios
Preterm contractions or prelabour rupture of membranes
Malpresentation or a high, unstable lie near term, carrying a cord prolapse risk
Sonographic evidence of a major fetal anomaly, hydrops, or twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Signs of placental abruption after membrane rupture
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic mild polyhydramnios generally has a good outcome, but moderate-to-severe polyhydramnios and cases with an identifiable fetal anomaly or twin-to-twin transfusion carry higher perinatal morbidity and mortality; prognosis is largely determined by the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Labelling polyhydramnios idiopathic without a thorough search for fetal anomaly, diabetes, and anaemia
Overlooking oesophageal atresia antenatally and failing to assess the neonate, for example by passing a nasogastric tube, after birth
Performing artificial rupture of membranes without controlling for the risk of cord prolapse and abruption from sudden decompression
Neglecting the raised risk of postpartum haemorrhage from an overdistended, atonic uterus
Missing twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome by not assessing chorionicity and inter-twin discordance
references: ISUOG practice guidelines on fetal ultrasound and amniotic fluid assessment
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
